lesson.title: and: True Only When Both Sides Are
lesson.summary: The and operator combines two boolean expressions and evaluates to True only when both of them are True, modeling the everyday idea of two conditions that must both hold.
lesson.body:
and takes two boolean expressions, one on each side, and evaluates to True in exactly one situation: when the left side is True and the right side is also True. In every other combination, both False, left True and right False, or left False and right True, the result is False. This mirrors how the word "and" works in ordinary English. Saying "I will go to the park if it is sunny and I have free time" means both conditions have to hold; sunny weather alone is not enough if there is no free time, and free time alone is not enough if it is raining.

Because and always operates on two boolean expressions, and those expressions are frequently comparisons, the ideas from earlier in this chapter combine naturally. A single and expression can enforce a range, a set of requirements, or any situation where multiple things must simultaneously be true, without needing separate if statements for each condition.

Trace this login check carefully:

username_ok = True
password_length = 10
strong_enough = username_ok and password_length >= 8
print(strong_enough)

Python evaluates the right side, password_length >= 8, substituting 10 for password_length, which gives 10 >= 8, a True result. The left side, username_ok, is already the boolean value True. and now combines True and True. Since both sides are True, the entire expression evaluates to True, and that is what strong_enough is bound to. If password_length had instead been 5, the right side would evaluate to False, and and would produce False overall regardless of the left side, since both sides are required to be True for and to succeed.

A frequent point of confusion for new programmers is writing something like if 5 < x < 10, expecting Python to somehow understand that both ends need checking, without realizing the same effect can be written explicitly with and: x > 5 and x < 10. That explicit and version shows directly what is happening: two separate boolean expressions are each evaluated, then combined with the requirement that both must hold. Chained comparisons like 5 < x < 10, covered later in this chapter, turn out to work by essentially this same and based logic under the hood.

and is not restricted to combining exactly two boolean expressions; Python allows longer chains such as a and b and c, which evaluates as though written (a and b) and c, requiring every single expression in the chain to be True before the whole line can be True. This makes and a natural way to enforce several independent requirements at once, such as checking that a number is positive, even, and less than 100 all in a single line: n > 0 and n % 2 == 0 and n < 100. For n equal to 50, each piece evaluates in turn: 50 > 0 is True, 50 % 2 == 0 is True since 50 divides evenly by 2 with no remainder, and 50 < 100 is True, so the whole chain evaluates to True.
